newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya reform leaders urge support for crusade.
newsitem.headline: Kenya reform leaders urge support for crusade.

text.p: Leaders of a political reform campaign in Kenya urged supporters on Friday not to abandon a crusade for change in the face of Kenya's ruling party seeking to hijack their demands.

The ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party on Thursday proposed measures that could effectively pull the reform rug from under an opposition-backed alliance, which had forged rare unity among opponents of President Daniel arap Moi.
The proposals surprised opposition leaders and stunned many ordinary Kenyans, the backbone since June of rallies and clashes with riot police that hit tourism and scared foreign investors.

"They (KANU) have dented the pressure," admitted Willy Mutunga, a leader of an alliance of opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies campaigning for reforms before elections this year. "It's up to us to make the next move."
Opposition leaders urged 400 supporters at an open-air service for the dead from clashes this month to stick to the campaign they hoped would unseat Moi, 73, and in power for 19 years.
"The freedom we have fought for has not been restored," said Democratic Party chief Mwai Kibaki. "Struggle to the very end."

"Moi is now acting out of weakness. Moi will not beat us. We will win...When we fight for change we don't want Moi to give it to us. We want to win it ourselves," James Orengo, the deputy opposition leader in parliament, told a cheering crowd.
Police remained out of sight as what was billed as a memorial service with the bodies of two of the dead in coffins at the feet of speakers turned at times into a political rally.

KANU's National Executive Council chaired by Moi proposed on Thursday parliament pass a bill for 11 controversial laws to be "repealed or amended where deemed necessary" before elections and to set up a commission to review Kenya's constitution.

If enacted by parliament, where KANU has a majority, the repeal of the 11 laws, some dating back to the colonial period, would reduce Moi's power. But it would also remove a main pillar of the reform drive and possibly split the opposition again.
Moi has been tipped to win another five-year term and could move to catch the opposition off guard after losing its common cause by calling elections shortly after repealing the 11 laws.

Opposition FORD-Asili party chairman Kenneth Matiba in a statement accused Moi of using the tactics of "divide and rule" and said his party would only accept a constitutional conference and not "legal reforms which KANU is giving the country".

Opposition National Development party leader Raila Odinga said Moi wanted to divide the opposition by "musical chairs" but his party would examine any government reform package before deciding whether he should stand as a presidential candidate.
"KANU recognises it is in a tight corner over reforms. It has found it necessary to make some concessions," said Odinga, citing three demands he said were not covered by KANU reforms.
"KANU thinks it can pull the wool over our eyes," he said.

"I am apprehensive. KANU is trying to stem the crisis, not to change genuinely," said Reverend Timothy Njoya, a Presbyterian cleric who is a member of the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) which spearheaded the reform drive.

Njoya's arm was broken by police on July 7 during clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in Nairobi and several other cities and towns. At least nine people were killed in the worst political violence to hit Kenya in seven years.

KANU's proposals were announced after the NCEC called for a series of new "mass actions" including a rally in Kenya's second city Mombasa, the centre of its coast tourism industry, on July 26 and a nationwide general strike and sit-in on August 8.
